title: John Cassavetes
wiki_lead:
John Nicholas Cassavetes (December 9, 1929 – February 3, 1989) was a Greek-American filmmaker and actor. He began as an actor in film and television before helping to pioneer modern American independent cinema as a writer and director, often self-financing, producing, and distributing his own films. He received nominations for three Academy Awards, two BAFTA Awards, four Golden Globe Awards, and an Emmy Award.
After studying at the American Academy of Dramatic Arts, Cassavetes started his career in television acting in numerous network dramas. From 1959 to 1960 he played the title role in the NBC detective series Johnny Staccato. He acted in notable films, such as Martin Ritt's film noir Edge of the City (1957), Robert Aldrich's war film The Dirty Dozen (1967), Roman Polanski's horror film Rosemary's Baby (1968) and Elaine May's crime drama Mikey and Nicky (1976). For The Dirty Dozen, he earned a nomination for the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor.
As a director, Cassavetes became known for a string of critically acclaimed independent dramas including Shadows (1959), Faces (1968), Husbands (1970), A Woman Under the Influence (1974), Opening Night (1977), and Love Streams (1984). His films employed an actor-centered approach which prioritized raw character relationships, "small feelings", and "messy anguish [that] sanctifies," while rejecting traditional Hollywood plotting, method acting, and stylization. His films became associated with an improvisational aesthetic and a cinéma vérité feel. He received Academy Award nominations for Best Original Screenplay (Faces) and Best Director (A Woman Under the Influence). Shadows, Faces, and A Woman Under the Influence have been inducted into the National Film Registry.
He frequently collaborated with American actress Gena Rowlands, to whom he was married from 1954 until his death in 1989, and friends Peter Falk, Ben Gazzara, and Seymour Cassel. Many of his films were shot and edited in his and Rowlands' own Los Angeles home. He and Rowlands had a son, Nick, and two daughters, Alexandra and Zoe, all of whom followed them into acting and filmmaking.

Early life and education
John Nicholas Cassavetes was born in New York City on December 9, 1929, the son of Greek-American actress Katherine Cassavetes (née Demetriou), who was later featured in some of his films, and Greek immigrant Nicholas John Cassavetes. His early years were spent with his family in Greece; when he returned to New York at the age of seven, he spoke no English. He was then raised on Long Island, where he attended Paul D. Schreiber Senior High School (then known as Port Washington High School) from 1945 to 1947 and participated in Port Weekly (the school paper), Red Domino (interclass play), football, and the Port Light (yearbook).

Born in New York City to Greek immigrant parents, he grew up in an upper-middle-class household on Long Island and studied acting at the American Academy of Dramatic Arts. Cassavetes directed twelve feature films, often financing them through his acting income to maintain creative control outside the Hollywood studio system, and collaborated frequently with his wife, actress Gena Rowlands, whom he married in 1954. He died in Los Angeles at age 59 from complications of cirrhosis of the liver. Cassavetes began his career in the 1950s acting in live television dramas during the Golden Age of TV, appearing in shows like Studio One and Kraft Television Theatre, before transitioning to film with roles in features such as Edge of the City (1957) alongside Sidney Poitier. His acting breakthrough came with an Academy Award nomination for Best Supporting Actor for his role as a convict in The Dirty Dozen (1967), and he later starred in prominent Hollywood films including Rosemary's Baby (1968) as an aspiring actor, The Fury (1978), and Whose Life Is It Anyway? (1981). These roles provided financial stability, allowing him to self-finance his directorial projects and avoid studio interference that he deeply resented. As a director, Cassavetes debuted with Shadows (1959), shot on a shoestring budget with non-professional actors using improvisation, which won the Critics' Award at the 1960 Venice Film Festival and is credited with launching the American independent film movement. His subsequent films, characterized by long takes, naturalistic dialogue, and extended production periodsâoften involving multiple versions and reshootsâinclude Faces (1968), which earned three Academy Award nominations, including for Best Original Screenplay; Husbands (1970), examining male friendship and midlife crisis; Minnie and Moskowitz (1971); and A Woman Under the Influence (1974), a poignant study of mental illness starring Rowlands, for which Cassavetes received Academy Award nominations for Best Director and Best Original Screenplay, while Rowlands was nominated for Best Actress. Later works like The Killing of a Chinese Bookie (1976), Opening Night (1977), Love Streams (1984), and Gloria (1980)âthe latter winning the Golden Lion at the Venice Film Festivalâcontinued his focus on personal, idiosyncratic narratives. Cassavetes's influence extends to generations of filmmakers, including Martin Scorsese and the Coen brothers, who adopted his emphasis on authenticity and character-driven storytelling in independent cinema. He and Rowlands raised three childrenâ Nick, Alexandra, and Zoeâall of whom pursued careers in film, with Nick directing She's So Lovely (1997) from one of his father's unproduced screenplays. His archives, including early versions of films like the lost 1957 cut of Shadows rediscovered in 2002, continue to reveal his experimental process and enduring legacy as a transformative figure in American cinema, evidenced by recent retrospectives such as a complete series of his films in Australia in 2024 and a program on his collaborations with Gena Rowlands at the Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive in May 2025.
